blogs.subtitle: A step-by-step look at setting up an automated CI/CD pipeline to build and submit React Native apps to the Apple App Store and Google Play Store whenever a new version is merged into the development branch.

blocks.content:
Releasing a mobile app by hand gets old fast: bump the version, run a build for iOS, run another for Android, wait, download, upload to App Store Connect, upload to Play Console… and repeat for every release.

In this post I'll show how I automated the whole thing with GitHub Actions and EAS (Expo Application Services). The rule is simple: when a branch is merged into dev and the app version went up (for example 1.0.0 → 1.0.1), GitHub Actions builds the app for both platforms and EAS submits the builds to App Store Connect and Google Play. If the version didn't change, nothing gets built.

I'll also go through the problems I ran into along the way, including Google Cloud's "Service account key creation is disabled" error, and how I solved them.
What We're Building

The pipeline has four pieces:

A small Node script that compares the version in app.json before and after the merge.
A GitHub Actions workflow that runs on every push to dev and only continues if the version increased.
An eas.json configured with a production build profile and submit settings for both stores.
Store credentials saved on EAS (an App Store Connect API key for iOS, a Google Service Account key for Android) so builds can be submitted without anyone at the keyboard.
Prerequisites: an Expo project that already builds with EAS (eas build works locally), an Apple Developer account, a Google Play Console account, and an app that already exists in both stores.
Step 1: The Version Bump Checker

GitHub gives us the commit SHA from before the push (github.event.before). The script reads app.json at that commit and at the new HEAD, compares expo.version, and writes should_release=true or false as a step output for the rest of the workflow to use.

Create scripts/check-version-bump.mjs:

blocks.caption: scripts/check-version-bump.mjs

blocks.content: You can test it locally before pushing anything. Pass the old ref and the new ref:
ode scripts/check-version-bump.mjs origin/dev HEAD
blocks.caption: terminal

blocks.content:
should_release=true
old_version=1.0.0
new_version=1.0.1
blocks.caption: Tip: keep the version in package.json in sync with expo.version in app.json. The script only reads app.json, but having two different version numbers will confuse your team.

blocks.content: Step 2: The GitHub Actions Workflow

The workflow has three jobs. check-version always runs. The iOS and Android jobs only run when check-version says should_release is true, and they run in parallel. There's also a manual trigger (workflow_dispatch), so you can release just one platform from the Actions tab when you need to.

Create .github/workflows/auto-release.yml:

name: Auto Build & Submit to App Store and Play Store

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - dev
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      platform:
        description: "Platform(s) to build and submit"
        required: true
        default: "all"
        type: choice
        options:
          - all
          - ios
          - android

concurrency:
  group: eas-auto-release-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  check-version:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      should_release: ${{ steps.version.outputs.should_release }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - name: Compare version against previous commit
        id: version
        env:
          BEFORE_SHA: ${{ github.event.before }}
        run: node scripts/check-version-bump.mjs

  build-and-submit-ios:
    needs: check-version
    if: >-
      needs.check-version.outputs.should_release == 'true' &&
      (github.event_name != 'workflow_dispatch' ||
      github.event.inputs.platform == 'all' ||
      github.event.inputs.platform == 'ios')
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: "22"
          cache: "npm"
      - run: npm ci
      - uses: expo/expo-github-action@v8
        with:
          eas-version: latest
          token: ${{ secrets.EXPO_TOKEN }}
      - name: Build iOS & auto-submit to App Store Connect
        run: eas build --platform ios --profile production --auto-submit --non-interactive --no-wait

  build-and-submit-android:
    needs: check-version
    if: >-
      needs.check-version.outputs.should_release == 'true' &&
      (github.event_name != 'workflow_dispatch' ||
      github.event.inputs.platform == 'all' ||
      github.event.inputs.platform == 'android')
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: "22"
          cache: "npm"
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Restore google-services.json from secret
        env:
          GOOGLE_SERVICES_JSON: ${{ secrets.GOOGLE_SERVICES_JSON }}
        run: |
          if [ -n "$GOOGLE_SERVICES_JSON" ]; then
            printf '%s' "$GOOGLE_SERVICES_JSON" > google-services.json
            sed -i '/^google-services.json$/d' .gitignore
          fi
      - uses: expo/expo-github-action@v8
        with:
          eas-version: latest
          token: ${{ secrets.EXPO_TOKEN }}
      - name: Build Android & auto-submit to Google Play
        run: eas build --platform android --profile production --auto-submit --non-interactive --no-wait
blocks.caption: .github/workflows/auto-release.yml

blocks.content:
What the important flags do:

--auto-submit: as soon as the cloud build finishes, EAS starts a submission to the store using the submit profile with the same name (production).
--non-interactive: CI can't answer prompts, so every credential has to be stored on EAS already.
--no-wait: the GitHub job ends once the build is queued, so you don't burn Actions minutes waiting. Follow the build and submission progress on expo.dev instead.
node-version: use the Node version your Expo SDK requires.

Why the google-services.json step? That file is usually gitignored, so a fresh CI checkout doesn't have it. We write it from a GitHub secret. EAS skips gitignored files when it uploads your project, so the step also removes that line from .gitignore inside the CI runner only. Your real .gitignore isn't touched. A cleaner alternative is to store the file as an EAS "file" environment variable and point app.json at it.
Step 3: Configure eas.json
Three things matter here: Android must build an .aab (Google Play requires App Bundles), build numbers should increment automatically, and the submit profile needs to know where to send each build.

blocks.caption: eas.json

blocks.content:
appVersionSource: "remote" + autoIncrement: true: EAS manages the iOS buildNumber and Android versionCode and increments them on every build, so you only bump the human-readable version (1.0.0 → 1.0.1).
ascAppId: the numeric ID from your App Store URL (apps.apple.com/app/id YOUR_ASC_APP_ID).
track: which Play track receives the build: production, beta, alpha or internal.
releaseStatus: "draft" uploads the build without rolling it out, so you can add release notes and press Rollout yourself. Use "completed" to send it straight out.
Common mix-up: "internal" is a track, not a releaseStatus. To ship to internal testers automatically, set "track": "internal".
Step 4: GitHub Secrets

Go to GitHub → YOUR_GITHUB_ORG/YOUR_REPO → Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret and add:

EXPO_TOKEN: an access token so CI can run EAS commands as your account.
GOOGLE_SERVICES_JSON: the full contents of your google-services.json (only needed if your Android app uses Firebase, e.g. for push notifications).
Creating the EXPO_TOKEN with a robot user

Don't use your personal token. In your Expo organization (YOUR_EXPO_ORG), open the members/access-token settings, create a robot user (e.g. YOUR_ROBOT_USER) with the Developer role, and generate a token for it. If the token ever leaks, you can revoke it without touching anyone's personal account.
Never commit a token to the repo or paste it into a chat, a ticket or a screenshot. If one gets exposed, revoke it on expo.dev right away, generate a new one, and update the GitHub secret.
Step 5: iOS Credentials (App Store Connect API Key)
For --non-interactive submissions, EAS needs an App Store Connect API key so it never hits an Apple ID 2FA prompt. Run:

blocks.caption: terminal
blocks.content: npx eas credentials -p ios

Choose the production profile and log in to your Apple account. If the summary already lists an App Store Connect API Key, a Distribution Certificate and an active Provisioning Profile, iOS is ready. If no API key is listed, choose "App Store Connect: Manage your API Key" and let EAS create one.
Check the expiry dates on the distribution certificate and provisioning profile while you're in there. Put a reminder in your calendar a few weeks before they expire.
Step 6: Android Credentials (Google Play Service Account)
This was the longest part. Google Play only accepts automated uploads from a Google Cloud service account that has been invited into your Play Console.
6.1 Enable the API and create a service account

1. Open Google Cloud Console and select (or create) a project, e.g. YOUR_GCP_PROJECT_ID.
2. Search for "Google Play Android Developer API" and click Enable.
3. Go to IAM & Admin → Service Accounts → Create Service Account. Name it something like YOUR_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_NAME (description: "Automated Play Store submissions via EAS"). You can skip the optional role step.
4. Open the new account and copy its email: YOUR_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_NAME@YOUR_GCP_PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com
5. Open the Keys tab → Add Key → Create new key → JSON → Create. A .json file downloads.
6.2 Problem: "Service account key creation is disabled"
On step 5, I got this error instead of a download:
"Service account key creation is disabled" — an Organization Policy (iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation) is enforced on your organization.

Newer Google Cloud organizations get "Secure by Default" policies, and one of them blocks JSON key creation. If you're an admin of the organization, you can switch it off for this one project only:

1. Give yourself the Organization Policy Administrator role. This role only shows up at the organization level: in the top-left resource picker, select the organization (the building icon), not a project. Then go to IAM & Admin → IAM, edit your account, and add Organization Policy Administrator.
2. Switch the picker back to your project (YOUR_GCP_PROJECT_ID) and go to IAM & Admin → Organization Policies.
3. Open "Disable service account key creation" (iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation) → Manage policy.
4. Select "Override parent's policy" → Add a rule → Enforcement: Off → Done → Set policy.
5. Wait about a minute and create the JSON key again. It should download this time.

If you aren't an org admin, either ask the admin to do the steps above, or create the service account in a Google Cloud project that isn't under an organization. Play Console accepts a service account from any project.
6.3 Invite the service account into Play Console

1. Open Google Play Console → Users and permissions → Invite new users.
2. Paste the service account email.
3. Under App permissions → Add app → select YOUR_APP_NAME (COM.YOURCOMPANY.YOURAPP).
4. Grant at least: View app information (read-only), Release to production / exclude devices / use Play App Signing, Release apps to testing tracks, and Manage testing tracks.
5. Click Invite user. Service accounts are accepted automatically.
6.4 Upload the key to EAS
npx eas credentials -p android

production
→ Google Service Account
→ Manage your Google Service Account Key for Play Store Submissions
→ Set up a new service account key
→ select the downloaded .json file
When it's done, the credentials summary should show "Submissions: Google Service Account Key for Play Store Submissions" with your service account email.

Once the key is on EAS, delete the .json file from your machine (or move it into a password manager), and add a pattern like YOUR_GCP_PROJECT_ID-*.json to .gitignore so it can never be committed by accident. If you only switched the org policy off to create this key, consider switching it back on.
Step 7: Ship It

The day-to-day flow is now:

1. Work on your feature branch.
2. Bump the version in app.json (and package.json), e.g. 1.0.0 → 1.0.1.
3. Merge into dev.

GitHub Actions detects the bump and starts both builds. Watch them at expo.dev → YOUR_EXPO_ORG / YOUR_EXPO_PROJECT → Builds and Submissions.
What happens after the upload
iOS

The build is uploaded to App Store Connect and shows up in TestFlight after Apple processes it (usually 10–20 minutes). EAS does not send it for review. Open App Store Connect, attach the build to your new version, and click Submit for Review.
Android

The .aab goes to the track you configured. With releaseStatus "draft", open Play Console → your track → edit the draft release, add release notes, and start the rollout. Switch to "completed" once you trust the pipeline enough to skip that step.
Gotcha: Google Play's API can't create the very first release of an app. If your app has never been uploaded, upload the first .aab manually in Play Console. Automated submissions work from then on.
Troubleshooting Checklist

The workflow ran but both store jobs were skipped → the version didn't increase. Check the reason output of the check-version job.
The EAS step fails with an auth error → EXPO_TOKEN is missing or revoked, or the robot user lacks permission in the organization.
The iOS submit fails → there's no App Store Connect API key on EAS, or ascAppId is wrong.
The Android submit fails with a permission error → the service account wasn't invited in Play Console, or it doesn't have release permissions for this app.
The Android build fails because google-services.json is missing → the GOOGLE_SERVICES_JSON secret is empty or isn't valid JSON.
Wrapping Up

With one script, one workflow and a one-time credentials setup, a release now means bumping a version number and merging. Builds are consistent, nobody uploads binaries by hand, and the store review step stays under your control.

If you try this and get stuck, Contact me or chat. I'm happy to help.

blocks.content: Why React Native + Expo Scales Fast

Building production mobile applications across iOS and Android demands predictable release pipelines, rock-solid native integrations, and fast iteration cycles. Across projects like Dealrax, Doc4Baby, PlayZone, and Mangaliyam, Expo EAS builds dramatically reduced store submission friction.
Good mobile architecture isn’t just about screens — it’s reliable push notifications, resilient offline sync, and clean payment flows.
Production Release Checklist

Always verify deep-link handling, test PayHere and third-party payment callbacks on physical devices, and validate push notification payloads in background, killed, and foreground states before submitting to App Store Connect or Play Console.
